title: How Not To Feel Resentment Over Difficult Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin acknowledges that resentment toward a chronically disruptive student is a normal feeling but insists it always leaks out, visible to the student even when a teacher tries to hide it. Building on earlier advice about choosing to like difficult students, he addresses teachers who genuinely try but still can't shake their animosity in the moment a student disrupts a good lesson. His proposed solution is a reframe: a difficult student's behavior is rarely truly about the teacher, but rather the residue of being let down by adults, permissiveness, abuse, neglect, poverty, or other trauma, which surfaces most acutely around any authority figure. Recognizing this, he argues, replaces resentment with compassion without lowering standards or excusing accountability, since love in his framing is 'the active pursuit of what's best for another' rather than an emotion. Once students sense this genuine reframe, he writes, their behavior changes.
points: Resentment toward difficult students is described as a natural feeling that inevitably becomes visible to the student, no matter how well hidden.
The article specifically addresses teachers who genuinely try to like difficult students but still feel animosity resurface in moments of disruption.
The recommended reframe: a student's hostility toward the teacher is usually the residue of being let down by adults, not a personal attack.
This reframe is said to replace resentment with compassion and understanding without lowering standards or accountability.
Love is defined not as an emotion but as 'the active pursuit of what's best for another,' which students can sense once it is genuine.
quotes: It’s normal to feel angry. How could you not? You have a student who is ruining your school year.
If you’re a regular reader of SCM, however, then you know that resentment does you no good. In fact, it makes things worse because it’s something you can’t hide, no matter how hard you try.
The solution is to realize that it’s not the student’s fault. Somewhere along the line they’ve been let down by the adults in their life.
That’s not to say that they’re not responsible for their own behavior. They are, 100%. But you’re the one standing in front of them.
Grasping this reality has a way of putting things into perspective and replacing the resentment you can’t seem to shake with compassion and understanding.
This doesn’t mean that you’ll ever lower your standards or fail to hold them accountable. Love, after all, is not an emotion. Rather, it’s the active pursuit of what’s best for another.
